msg: chore(release): v1.27.2 — l'espace public prend son identité (ADR-181)
old:
Was ist ein Skill?

Ein Skill ist ein Satz strukturierter Anweisungen, der LIA ermöglicht, einen bestimmten Bereich zu beherrschen. Im Gegensatz zu Tools, die Aktionen ausführen, bereichern Skills das Reasoning und Verhalten des Assistenten. Die Architektur basiert auf einem Schlüsselprinzip: Die Festplatte ist die Wahrheitsquelle für Skill-Inhalte, während die Datenbank nur Metadaten verwaltet (Aktivierung, Eigentümer, Statistiken).

Angereicherte Ausgaben (v1.16.8)

Seit v1.16.8 kann ein Python-Skript zusätzlich zum Text einen interaktiven HTML-Frame (Google Maps-Ansicht, Wetter-Dashboard, Pomodoro-Timer...) und/oder ein Bild (QR-Code, Diagramm) zurückgeben. Der Vertrag ist einfach: Das Skript schreibt ein JSON-Objekt auf stdout (SkillScriptOutput) mit den Feldern text (Pflicht), frame und image — unabhängig und kombinierbar. Frames werden in einem strengen Sandbox-iframe mit einer automatisch injizierten Content Security Policy für Benutzer-Skills ausgeführt. Theme und Sprache werden live via postMessage synchronisiert. Sieben neue integrierte Skills zeigen den Mechanismus: interactive-map, weather-dashboard, calendar-month, qr-code, pomodoro-timer, unit-converter, dice-roller.

Drei Skill-Typen

  • Prompt Expert — Detaillierte Anweisungen für eine Domäne (z.B. professionelles Schreiben, Finanzanalyse)
  • Advisory — Tipps und Best Practices (z.B. Stilratgeber, Qualitätscheckliste)
  • Plan Template — Ausführungsplan-Vorlagen für wiederkehrende Szenarien

Ausführung unter der Glasglocke

Ein Skill-Skript läuft in einem Container, der für diesen Aufruf entsteht und danach sofort verschwindet: kein Docker-Socket, --network none, ein schreibgeschütztes Root-Dateisystem mit kleinem beschreibbarem tmpfs, eine unprivilegierte Identität und alle Capabilities entzogen. Speicher, Prozessanzahl, CPU-Zeit und geschriebene Dateigröße sind gedeckelt.

Entscheidend ist, was ein Kindprozess erbt. Ein bloßer uid-Wechsel genügt nicht: In der Produktion gehört der Dienst zur docker-Gruppe, und eine Gruppe wird vererbt — der Socket bliebe erreichbar. Der Container beseitigt dieses Erbe konstruktiv. Und lässt sich die Sandbox nicht erzeugen, läuft das Skript gar nicht: Es gibt keinen Rückfall in einen schwächer geschützten Modus.

Der Quelltext des Skripts wird als Argument übergeben statt gemountet, was stdin für die JSON-Nutzlast frei hält — der Ein-/Ausgabevertrag der Skills bleibt unverändert.

Strukturiertes Ergebnis

Jede Skill-Ausführung gibt ein standardisiertes ScriptResult-Objekt zurück mit: success (Boolean), output (stdout), error (stderr), exit_code und execution_time_ms. Dieses Format ermöglicht eine einheitliche Behandlung von Erfolgen und Fehlern.

SkillBypassStrategy: Den Planer umgehen

Wenn ein deterministischer Skill genau zur Anfrage passt, umgeht die SkillBypassStrategy den LLM-Planer. Der Skill wird direkt ausgeführt, ohne die Kette Planer → Validator → Orchestrator zu durchlaufen, was Latenz und Token-Verbrauch reduziert.

Planer-Skill-Guard

Der Planer verfügt über eine Früherkennung, die bei fehlenden Pflichtparametern nach Klärung fragt. Multi-Domain-deterministische Skills (z.B. tägliches Briefing = Events + Aufgaben + Wetter + E-Mails) können jedoch falsch-positive Klärungsanfragen auslösen. Der Skill-Guard erkennt, wenn ein deterministischer Skill eine hohe Domain-Überlappung mit der Anfrage hat, und lässt die vollständige Planer-Pipeline entscheiden.

Der Skill-Generator

LIA enthält einen integrierten Skill-Generator. Beschreiben Sie die gewünschte Expertise in natürlicher Sprache, und LIA generiert automatisch einen strukturierten Skill im SKILL.md-Format, kompatibel mit dem Standard agentskills.io. Der fertige Skill wird validiert und direkt in Ihre Skills installiert — beim Namen genannt, sofort aktiv, ohne manuellen Upload.

Benutzerverwaltung

Jeder Benutzer kann seine Skills in der Oberfläche unter Einstellungen aktivieren, deaktivieren, importieren oder löschen — jetzt eine Galerie mit Vorschaubildern und deklarierten Ausgabekanälen (Text, interaktiver Frame, Bild). Der Import akzeptiert eine Datei oder eine serverseitig validierte https-URL (gleiche gehärtete Pipeline), und jede von außen importierte Skill trägt einen Herkunftshinweis. Administratoren können außerdem globale Skills definieren, die allen Benutzern zur Verfügung stehen.

Interaktive Widgets sind auf Dauer angelegt: Sie werden mit der Konversation gespeichert und öffnen sich nach einem Neuladen oder auf einem anderen Gerät wieder, und ein Frame, der nicht lädt, zeigt einen handlungsfähigen Fehlerzustand — Erklärung, Wiederholen, in neuem Tab öffnen — statt eines leeren Rechtecks.

Sehen, was eine Fähigkeit erzeugt

Die Detailansicht einer Fähigkeit zeigt jetzt eine Vorschau ihres Ergebnisses — ein Monatsraster, einen QR-Code, Wetterkarten — statt eines generischen Symbols. Diese Vorschaubilder werden generiert, nicht von Hand gezeichnet: Ein versioniertes Skript hält eine Zeichnung je Fähigkeit vor, in reiner Geometrie und ohne Schriftart-Abhängigkeit, wodurch die Ausgabe auf allen Maschinen identisch ist. Eine Prüfung schlägt fehl, wenn einer Fähigkeit die Zeichnung fehlt oder das ausgelieferte Bild nicht mehr dem entspricht, was ihr Generator erzeugt.

Eine Fähigkeit ändern, nicht nur erstellen

Eine Fähigkeit zu erstellen war nur halb nützlich, solange man sie nie wieder anfassen konnte. LIA kann nun eine Ihrer Fähigkeiten im Gespräch anpassen, erweitern oder korrigieren. Sie liest das vollständige Paket erneut — Manifest, Skripte, Referenzdokumente —, wendet Ihren Wunsch an und erzeugt dann das Ganze neu, statt an einer Stelle zu flicken. Diese Entscheidung ist kein Implementierungsdetail: Beschreibung, Skripte und Ressourcen einer Fähigkeit entwickeln sich gemeinsam, und eine nur an einer Stelle angewandte Korrektur erzeugt ein Paket, das sich selbst widerspricht.

Vor dem Schreiben zeigt LIA, was ersetzt wird und was verschwindet, und wartet auf ausdrückliche Zustimmung. Diese Bestätigung beruht nicht auf dem guten Willen des Modells: Sie verlangt ein aus dem Paketinhalt abgeleitetes Token, das nur eine erste Ablehnung liefern kann. Das Modell kann sie also nicht umgehen, und was Sie freigeben, ist genau das, was geschrieben wird. Mitgelieferte Bilder überleben ohnehin: Der Chat transportiert nur Text, also kopiert der Server sie aus der ersetzten Fassung zurück.

• Keine Farbe: Gelesene E-Mail (keine besondere Markierung)
• 🟠 Orange: Gelesen und wichtig (von Gmail als wichtig markiert)
• 🟢 Grün: Ungelesene E-Mail (neue Nachricht zum Lesen)
• 🔴 Rot: Ungelesen UND wichtig (hohe Priorität)

💡 Gut zu wissen:
• Der Status "wichtig" wird automatisch von Gmail basierend auf Ihren Gewohnheiten vergeben
• Ungelesene E-Mails haben auch ihren Betreff fett für bessere Sichtbarkeit
• Das "Ungelesen"-Abzeichen erscheint auch in den Metadaten der Karte

🟢 Grün = Zu lesen | 🔴 Rot = Dringend | 🟠 Orange = Wichtig bereits gelesen | Transparent = Bereits gelesen

msg: chore(release): prepare v2.0.0
old:
Für jede Aktion, die deine Daten ändert (erstellen, bearbeiten, löschen, senden), verwendet LIA ein Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)-System:

1. LIA erstellt einen Entwurf der Aktion
2. Du siehst eine Karte mit allen Feldern (Empfänger, Betreff, Text…)
3. Du kannst: Genehmigen, Bearbeiten oder Abbrechen
4. Die Aktion wird erst nach deiner ausdrücklichen Genehmigung ausgeführt

So behältst du immer die volle Kontrolle über Änderungen an deinen Daten.

📚 Mehrere Entwürfe auf einmal:
Bitte in einem Satz um zwei E-Mails: LIA listet zuerst auf, was sie vorbereitet hat, und zeigt dann einen Entwurf nach dem anderen ("Entwurf 1 von 2"), jeden mit eigener Karte und eigenem Genehmigen / Bearbeiten / Abbrechen. Nichts geht raus, bevor du zuletzt geantwortet hast, und der Bericht sagt, an wen und was gesendet wurde — ein abgebrochener Entwurf steht auch darin. Eine Massenaktion, die du als Liste genehmigt hast ("lösche diese 5 E-Mails"), behält eine einzige Bestätigung.

✉️ Eine Ausnahme:
Eine E-Mail an dich selbst geht ohne Entwurf hinaus: Ihr Empfänger ist deine eigene Adresse, die nichts ändern kann — nicht einmal ein Text, der in eine von LIA gelesene E-Mail geschmuggelt wurde.

new:
Um deine Daten zu schützen, durchläuft jede ändernde Aktion ein Entwurfssystem:

🔒 So funktioniert es:
1. Du forderst eine Aktion an ("Sende eine E-Mail an Hans")
2. LIA bereitet einen Entwurf vor
3. Du siehst eine Karte mit allen Feldern (Empfänger, Betreff, Text …)
4. Drei Möglichkeiten:
• ✅ Genehmigen: Die Aktion wird ausgeführt
• ✏️ Bearbeiten: den Entwurf korrigieren
• ❌ Abbrechen: Es passiert nichts

📋 Betroffene Aktionen:
• Senden, Beantworten, Weiterleiten von E-Mails
• Erstellen, Ändern, Löschen von Terminen
• Erstellen, Ändern von Kontakten
• Erstellen, Erledigen von Aufgaben
• Löschen von E-Mails

🛡️ Vorteile:
• Überprüfung vor jeder wichtigen Aktion
• Fehler lassen sich korrigieren
• Volle Kontrolle über deine Daten
• Keine unumkehrbare Aktion ohne deine Zustimmung

📚 Mehrere Entwürfe auf einmal:
Bitte in einem Satz um zwei E-Mails: LIA listet zuerst auf, was sie vorbereitet hat, und zeigt dann einen Entwurf nach dem anderen ("Entwurf 1 von 2"), jeden mit eigener Karte und eigenem Genehmigen / Bearbeiten / Abbrechen. Nichts wird gesendet, bevor du den letzten beantwortet hast, und der Bericht sagt, was an wen gegangen ist — auch ein abgebrochener Entwurf steht darin. Eine Massenaktion, die du als Liste genehmigt hast ("lösche diese 5 E-Mails"), behält eine einzige Bestätigung.

✉️ Eine Ausnahme:
Eine E-Mail an dich selbst geht ohne Entwurf hinaus: Ihr Empfänger ist deine eigene Adresse, und daran kann nichts etwas ändern — nicht einmal ein Text, der in eine E-Mail geschmuggelt wurde, die LIA liest.

old:
Para cualquier acción que modifique tus datos (crear, editar, eliminar, enviar), LIA usa un sistema Human-in-the-Loop (HITL):

1. LIA genera un borrador de la acción
2. Ves una tarjeta con todos los campos (destinatario, asunto, cuerpo…)
3. Puedes: Aprobar, Editar, o Cancelar
4. La acción solo se ejecuta después de tu aprobación explícita

Así siempre tienes el control total sobre los cambios en tus datos.

📚 Varios borradores a la vez:
Pide dos emails en una misma frase: LIA lista primero lo que preparó y luego muestra un borrador cada vez ("Borrador 1 de 2"), cada uno con su tarjeta y sus propios Aprobar / Editar / Cancelar. Para proteger tus datos, toda acción de modificación pasa por un sistema de borradores:

🔒 Cómo funciona:
1. Pides una acción ("Envía un correo a Juan")
2. LIA prepara un borrador
3. Ves una tarjeta con todos los campos (destinatario, asunto, cuerpo…)

• Creación y modificación de contactos
• Creación y finalización de tareas
• Eliminación de correos

• Verificación antes de cada acción importante
• Posibilidad de corregir errores
• Control total sobre tus datos
• Ninguna acción irreversible sin tu acuerdo

📚 Varios borradores a la vez:

Qu'est-ce qu'un skill ?

Un skill est un ensemble d'instructions structurées qui permet à LIA de maîtriser un domaine spécifique. Contrairement aux outils qui exécutent des actions, les skills enrichissent le raisonnement et le comportement de l'assistant. L'architecture repose sur un principe clé : le disque est la source de vérité pour le contenu des skills, tandis que la base de données gère uniquement les métadonnées (activation, propriétaire, statistiques).

Cinq archétypes de skills

  • Prompt Expert — Instructions détaillées pour un domaine (ex : rédaction professionnelle, analyse financière)
  • Advisory — Conseils et bonnes pratiques (ex : guide de style, checklist qualité)
  • Plan Template — Modèles de plans d'exécution pour des scénarios récurrents
  • Visualizer (v1.16.8) — Script Python qui produit une iframe interactive (carte, dashboard, calendrier)
  • Generator (v1.16.8) — Script Python qui produit une image (QR code, graphique)

Exécution sous cloche

Un script de skill s'exécute dans un conteneur créé pour cet appel et détruit juste après : pas de socket Docker, --network none, système de fichiers racine en lecture seule avec un petit tmpfs inscriptible, identité non privilégiée et toutes les capacités larguées. Mémoire, nombre de processus, temps CPU et taille des fichiers écrits sont plafonnés.

Ce qui compte ici, c'est ce qu'un processus fils hérite. Un simple changement d'uid ne suffit pas : en production le service appartient au groupe docker, et un groupe s'hérite — la socket resterait accessible. Le conteneur supprime cet héritage par construction. Et si le bac à sable ne peut pas être créé, le script ne tourne pas du tout : il n'existe aucun repli vers un mode moins protégé.

Le code source du script est passé en argument plutôt que monté, ce qui laisse stdin libre pour la charge JSON — le contrat d'entrée/sortie des skills reste identique.

Résultat structuré

Chaque exécution de skill retourne un objet ScriptResult standardisé contenant : success (booléen), output (stdout), error (stderr), exit_code et execution_time_ms. Ce format permet au système de traiter uniformément les succès et les erreurs.

Sorties enrichies (v1.16.8)

Depuis la v1.16.8, un script Python peut retourner — en plus du texte — une frame HTML interactive (carte Google Maps, dashboard météo, minuteur pomodoro...) et/ou une image (QR code, graphique). Le contrat est simple : le script écrit un JSON sur stdout (SkillScriptOutput) avec les champs text (obligatoire), frame et image, indépendants et combinables. Les frames tournent dans une iframe sandbox stricte (allow-scripts allow-popups ; allow-same-origin est réservé aux embeds des skills système de confiance comme la carte interactive, qui en ont besoin pour charger leurs propres données), avec une Content Security Policy injectée automatiquement pour les skills utilisateur — les skills système sont exemptés (admin de confiance). Thème et langue sont synchronisés en temps réel via postMessage : basculer en mode sombre se propage immédiatement dans chaque frame sans rechargement. Sept nouveaux skills intégrés démontrent le mécanisme : interactive-map, weather-dashboard, calendar-month, qr-code, pomodoro-timer, unit-converter, dice-roller.

SkillBypassStrategy : contourner le planificateur

Quand un skill déterministe correspond exactement à la demande, la SkillBypassStrategy court-circuite le planificateur LLM. Le skill est exécuté directement sans passer par la chaîne planner → validator → orchestrator, ce qui réduit la latence et la consommation de tokens.

Garde planificateur pour skills

Le planificateur dispose d'une détection précoce qui demande des clarifications lorsque des paramètres obligatoires sont manquants. Cependant, les skills déterministes multi-domaines (ex : briefing quotidien = événements + tâches + météo + emails) peuvent déclencher des faux positifs de clarification. La garde skill détecte quand un skill déterministe a un fort chevauchement de domaines avec la requête et laisse le pipeline planificateur complet décider au lieu de court-circuiter vers la clarification.

Le Skill Generator

LIA inclut un générateur de skills intégré. Décris le domaine d'expertise souhaité en langage naturel, et LIA génère automatiquement un skill structuré au format SKILL.md compatible avec le standard agentskills.io — y compris les nouveaux archétypes Visualizer et Generator avec les conventions runtime (thème, langue, auto-resize). La skill terminée est validée et installée directement dans tes skills — annoncée par son nom, active immédiatement, sans upload manuel.

Gestion par l'utilisateur

Chaque utilisateur peut activer, désactiver, importer ou supprimer ses skills dans l'interface Réglages — désormais une galerie avec images d'aperçu et canaux de sortie déclarés (texte, cadre interactif, image). L'import accepte un fichier ou une URL https validée côté serveur (même pipeline durci), et toute skill importée de l'extérieur porte un avertissement de provenance. Les administrateurs peuvent également définir des skills globaux disponibles pour tous les utilisateurs.

Les widgets interactifs sont faits pour durer : ils sont conservés avec la conversation et se rouvrent après un rechargement ou sur un autre appareil, et une frame qui ne charge pas affiche un état d'erreur actionnable — explication, réessayer, ouvrir dans un nouvel onglet — plutôt qu'un rectangle vide.

Voir ce qu'une compétence produit

La fiche d'une compétence montre désormais un aperçu de son résultat — une grille de mois, un code QR, des cartes météo — plutôt qu'une icône générique. Ces vignettes sont générées, pas dessinées à la main : un script versionné tient un dessin par compétence, en géométrie pure et sans dépendance de police, ce qui rend la sortie identique d'une machine à l'autre. Une garde échoue si une compétence n'a pas de dessin, ou si l'image livrée ne correspond plus à ce que son générateur produit.

Modifier une compétence, pas seulement en créer une

Créer une compétence ne servait qu'à moitié tant qu'on ne pouvait pas la reprendre. LIA sait désormais ajuster, enrichir ou corriger l'une des vôtres, en conversation. Elle relit le paquet complet — manifeste, scripts, documents de référence — applique ta demande, puis régénère l'ensemble plutôt que d'y faire une retouche ponctuelle. Ce choix n'est pas un détail d'implémentation : la description, les scripts et les ressources d'une compétence évoluent ensemble, et un correctif appliqué à un seul endroit produit un paquet qui se contredit.

Avant d'écrire, LIA présente ce qui sera remplacé et ce qui disparaîtra, et attend un accord explicite. Cette confirmation ne repose pas sur la bonne volonté du modèle : elle exige un jeton dérivé du contenu du paquet, que seul un premier refus peut fournir. Le modèle ne peut donc pas la contourner, et ce que tu approuves est exactement ce qui sera écrit. Les images embarquées, elles, survivent d'office : le chat ne transporte que du texte, alors le serveur les recopie depuis la version remplacée.

Plugins : des skills qui voyagent avec leurs serveurs

Les skills arrivent aussi par boîte entière : LIA parle le standard ouvert Agent Plugins (agent-plugins.org), le format de paquet portable adopté par ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot et VS Code, qui regroupe skills et serveurs MCP. Un plugin s’installe en une étape — zip ou lien https — via exactement le même pipeline durci qu’un skill individuel, et l’installation rapporte chaque composant : installé, mis à jour, ignoré avec sa raison, retiré. Désinstallez le plugin : tout ce qu’il avait apporté repart avec lui.
new:
Qu'est-ce qu'un skill ?

Un skill est un ensemble d'instructions structurées qui permet à LIA de maîtriser un domaine spécifique. Contrairement aux outils qui exécutent des actions, les skills enrichissent le raisonnement et le comportement de l'assistant. L'architecture repose sur un principe clé : le disque est la source de vérité pour le contenu des skills, tandis que la base de données gère uniquement les métadonnées (activation, propriétaire, statistiques).

Cinq archétypes de skills

  • Prompt Expert — Instructions détaillées pour un domaine (ex : rédaction professionnelle, analyse financière)
  • Advisory — Conseils et bonnes pratiques (ex : guide de style, checklist qualité)
  • Plan Template — Modèles de plans d'exécution pour des scénarios récurrents
  • Visualizer (v1.16.8) — Script Python qui produit une iframe interactive (carte, dashboard, calendrier)
  • Generator (v1.16.8) — Script Python qui produit une image (QR code, graphique)

Exécution sous cloche

Un script de skill s'exécute dans un conteneur créé pour cet appel et détruit juste après : pas de socket Docker, --network none, système de fichiers racine en lecture seule avec un petit tmpfs inscriptible, identité non privilégiée et toutes les capacités larguées. Mémoire, nombre de processus, temps CPU et taille des fichiers écrits sont plafonnés.

Ce qui compte ici, c'est ce qu'un processus fils hérite. Un simple changement d'uid ne suffit pas : en production le service appartient au groupe docker, et un groupe s'hérite — la socket resterait accessible. Le conteneur supprime cet héritage par construction. Et si le bac à sable ne peut pas être créé, le script ne tourne pas du tout : il n'existe aucun repli vers un mode moins protégé.

Le code source du script est passé en argument plutôt que monté, ce qui laisse stdin libre pour la charge JSON — le contrat d'entrée/sortie des skills reste identique.

Résultat structuré

Chaque exécution de skill retourne un objet ScriptResult standardisé contenant : success (booléen), output (stdout), error (stderr), exit_code et execution_time_ms. Ce format permet au système de traiter uniformément les succès et les erreurs.

Sorties enrichies (v1.16.8)

Depuis la v1.16.8, un script Python peut retourner — en plus du texte — une frame HTML interactive (carte Google Maps, dashboard météo, minuteur pomodoro...) et/ou une image (QR code, graphique). Le contrat est simple : le script écrit un JSON sur stdout (SkillScriptOutput) avec les champs text (obligatoire), frame et image, indépendants et combinables. Les frames tournent dans une iframe sandbox stricte (allow-scripts allow-popups ; allow-same-origin est réservé aux embeds des skills système de confiance comme la carte interactive, qui en ont besoin pour charger leurs propres données), avec une Content Security Policy injectée automatiquement pour les skills utilisateur — les skills système sont exemptés (admin de confiance). Thème et langue sont synchronisés en temps réel via postMessage : basculer en mode sombre se propage immédiatement dans chaque frame sans rechargement. Sept nouveaux skills intégrés démontrent le mécanisme : interactive-map, weather-dashboard, calendar-month, qr-code, pomodoro-timer, unit-converter, dice-roller.

SkillBypassStrategy : contourner le planificateur

Quand un skill déterministe correspond exactement à la demande, la SkillBypassStrategy court-circuite le planificateur LLM. Le skill est exécuté directement sans passer par la chaîne planner → validator → orchestrator, ce qui réduit la latence et la consommation de tokens.

Garde planificateur pour skills

Le planificateur dispose d'une détection précoce qui demande des clarifications lorsque des paramètres obligatoires sont manquants. Cependant, les skills déterministes multi-domaines (ex : briefing quotidien = événements + tâches + météo + emails) peuvent déclencher des faux positifs de clarification. La garde skill détecte quand un skill déterministe a un fort chevauchement de domaines avec la requête et laisse le pipeline planificateur complet décider au lieu de court-circuiter vers la clarification.

Le Skill Generator

LIA inclut un générateur de skills intégré. Décris le domaine d'expertise souhaité en langage naturel, et LIA génère automatiquement un skill structuré au format SKILL.md compatible avec le standard agentskills.io — y compris les nouveaux archétypes Visualizer et Generator avec les conventions runtime (thème, langue, auto-resize). La skill terminée est validée et installée directement dans tes skills — annoncée par son nom, active immédiatement, sans upload manuel.

Gestion par l'utilisateur

Chaque utilisateur peut activer, désactiver, importer ou supprimer ses skills dans l'interface Réglages — désormais une galerie avec images d'aperçu et canaux de sortie déclarés (texte, cadre interactif, image). L'import accepte un fichier ou une URL https validée côté serveur (même pipeline durci), et toute skill importée de l'extérieur porte un avertissement de provenance. Les administrateurs peuvent également définir des skills globaux disponibles pour tous les utilisateurs.

Les widgets interactifs sont faits pour durer : ils sont conservés avec la conversation et se rouvrent après un rechargement ou sur un autre appareil, et une frame qui ne charge pas affiche un état d'erreur actionnable — explication, réessayer, ouvrir dans un nouvel onglet — plutôt qu'un rectangle vide.

Voir ce qu'une compétence produit

La fiche d'une compétence montre désormais un aperçu de son résultat — une grille de mois, un code QR, des cartes météo — plutôt qu'une icône générique. Ces vignettes sont générées, pas dessinées à la main : un script versionné tient un dessin par compétence, en géométrie pure et sans dépendance de police, ce qui rend la sortie identique d'une machine à l'autre. Une garde échoue si une compétence n'a pas de dessin, ou si l'image livrée ne correspond plus à ce que son générateur produit.

Modifier une compétence, pas seulement en créer une

Créer une compétence ne servait qu'à moitié tant qu'on ne pouvait pas la reprendre. LIA sait désormais ajuster, enrichir ou corriger l'une des tiennes, en conversation. Elle relit le paquet complet — manifeste, scripts, documents de référence — applique ta demande, puis régénère l'ensemble plutôt que d'y faire une retouche ponctuelle. Ce choix n'est pas un détail d'implémentation : la description, les scripts et les ressources d'une compétence évoluent ensemble, et un correctif appliqué à un seul endroit produit un paquet qui se contredit.

Per qualsiasi azione che modifica i tuoi dati (creare, modificare, eliminare, inviare), LIA usa un sistema Human-in-the-Loop (HITL):

1. LIA genera una bozza dell'azione
2. Vedi una scheda con tutti i campi (destinatario, oggetto, corpo…)
3. Puoi: Approvare, Modificare o Annullare
4. L'azione viene eseguita solo dopo la tua approvazione esplicita

📚 Più bozze in una volta:
Chiedi due email in una stessa frase: LIA elenca prima ciò che ha preparato, poi mostra una bozza alla volta ("Bozza 1 di 2"), ciascuna con la sua scheda e i suoi Approva / Modifica / Annulla. old:
Cos'è uno skill?

Uno skill è un insieme di istruzioni strutturate che permette a LIA di padroneggiare un dominio specifico. A differenza degli strumenti che eseguono azioni, gli skill arricchiscono il ragionamento e il comportamento dell'assistente. L'architettura si basa su un principio chiave: il disco è la fonte di verità per il contenuto degli skill, mentre il database gestisce unicamente i metadati (attivazione, proprietario, statistiche).

Output arricchiti (v1.16.8)

Dalla v1.16.8, uno script Python può restituire — oltre al testo — un frame HTML interattivo (vista Google Maps, dashboard meteo, timer Pomodoro...) e/o un'immagine (QR code, grafico). Il contratto è semplice: lo script scrive un oggetto JSON su stdout (SkillScriptOutput) con i campi text (obbligatorio), frame e image — indipendenti e combinabili. I frame vengono eseguiti in un iframe sandbox rigoroso con una Content Security Policy iniettata automaticamente per le skill utente. Tema e lingua sono sincronizzati in tempo reale via postMessage. Sette nuove skill integrate illustrano il meccanismo: interactive-map, weather-dashboard, calendar-month, qr-code, pomodoro-timer, unit-converter, dice-roller.

Tre tipi di skill

  • Prompt Expert — Istruzioni dettagliate per un dominio (es.: redazione professionale, analisi finanziaria)
  • Advisory — Consigli e buone pratiche (es.: guida di stile, checklist qualità)
  • Plan Template — Modelli di piani di esecuzione per scenari ricorrenti

Esecuzione sotto campana

Uno script di skill viene eseguito in un container creato per quella chiamata e distrutto subito dopo: nessun socket Docker, --network none, filesystem radice in sola lettura con un piccolo tmpfs scrivibile, identità non privilegiata e tutte le capability rimosse. Memoria, numero di processi, tempo di CPU e dimensione dei file scritti sono limitati.

Ciò che conta qui è quel che un processo figlio eredita. Cambiare uid non basta: in produzione il servizio appartiene al gruppo docker, e un gruppo si eredita — il socket resterebbe raggiungibile. Il container elimina questa eredità per costruzione. E se la sandbox non può essere creata, lo script non gira affatto: non esiste alcun ripiego verso una modalità meno protetta.

Il sorgente dello script viene passato come argomento anziché montato, il che lascia stdin libero per il payload JSON — il contratto di input/output delle skill resta invariato.

Risultato strutturato

Ogni esecuzione di skill restituisce un oggetto ScriptResult standardizzato contenente: success (booleano), output (stdout), error (stderr), exit_code e execution_time_ms. Questo formato permette al sistema di trattare uniformemente successi ed errori.

SkillBypassStrategy: aggirare il pianificatore

Quando uno skill deterministico corrisponde esattamente alla richiesta, la SkillBypassStrategy cortocircuita il pianificatore LLM. Lo skill viene eseguito direttamente senza passare attraverso la catena planner → validator → orchestrator, riducendo la latenza e il consumo di token.

Guardia del pianificatore per skill

Il pianificatore dispone di un rilevamento precoce che richiede chiarimenti quando mancano parametri obbligatori. Tuttavia, gli skill deterministici multi-dominio (es.: briefing giornaliero = eventi + attività + meteo + email) possono attivare falsi positivi di chiarificazione. La guardia skill rileva quando uno skill deterministico ha un'alta sovrapposizione di domini con la query e lascia decidere alla pipeline completa del pianificatore.

Il Generatore di Skill

LIA include un generatore di skill integrato. Descrivi il dominio di competenza desiderato in linguaggio naturale, e LIA genera automaticamente uno skill strutturato nel formato SKILL.md compatibile con lo standard agentskills.io. La skill terminata viene validata e installata direttamente tra le tue skill — annunciata con il suo nome, subito attiva, senza upload manuale.

Gestione da parte dell'utente

Ogni utente può attivare, disattivare, importare o eliminare i propri skill nell'interfaccia Impostazioni — ora una galleria con immagini di anteprima e canali di output dichiarati (testo, frame interattivo, immagine). L'import accetta un file o un URL https validato lato server (stessa pipeline indurita), e ogni skill importata dall'esterno porta un avviso di provenienza. Gli amministratori possono anche definire skill globali disponibili per tutti gli utenti.

I widget interattivi sono fatti per durare: vengono conservati con la conversazione e si riaprono dopo un ricaricamento o su un altro dispositivo, e un frame che non carica mostra uno stato di errore azionabile — spiegazione, riprova, apri in una nuova scheda — invece di un rettangolo vuoto.

Vedere ciò che una competenza produce

La scheda di una competenza mostra ora un'anteprima del suo risultato — una griglia mensile, un codice QR, schede meteo — invece di un'icona generica. Quelle miniature sono generate, non disegnate a mano: uno script versionato tiene un disegno per competenza, in geometria pura e senza dipendenze da font, il che rende l'output identico su ogni macchina. Un controllo fallisce se una competenza non ha disegno, o se l'immagine distribuita non corrisponde più a quanto produce il suo generatore.

Modificare una competenza, non solo crearla

Creare una competenza serviva solo a metà finché non la si poteva riprendere. LIA sa ora adattare, arricchire o correggere una delle tue, conversando. Rilegge il pacchetto completo — manifesto, script, documenti di riferimento —, applica la tua richiesta, poi rigenera l'insieme invece di fare un ritocco puntuale. Questa scelta non è un dettaglio implementativo: descrizione, script e risorse di una competenza evolvono insieme, e una correzione applicata in un solo punto produce un pacchetto che si contraddice.

Prima di scrivere, LIA presenta cosa verrà sostituito e cosa scomparirà, e attende un consenso esplicito. Questa conferma non poggia sulla buona volontà del modello: richiede un token derivato dal contenuto del pacchetto, che solo un primo rifiuto può fornire. Il modello non può quindi aggirarla, e ciò che approvate è esattamente ciò che verrà scritto. Le immagini incluse sopravvivono d'ufficio: la chat trasporta solo testo, perciò il server le ricopia dalla versione sostituita.

Plugin: skill che viaggiano con i loro server

Le skill arrivano anche in blocco: LIA parla lo standard aperto Agent Plugins (agent-plugins.org), il formato di pacchetto portabile adottato da ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot e VS Code, che raggruppa skill e server MCP. Un plugin si installa in un passaggio — zip o link https — attraverso la stessa pipeline irrobustita di una skill individuale, e l'installazione riferisce ogni componente: installato, aggiornato, ignorato con il motivo, rimosso. Disinstalla il plugin e tutto ciò che aveva portato se ne va con lui.

new:
Per proteggere i tuoi dati, ogni azione di modifica passa per un sistema di bozze:

🔒 Come funziona:
1. Chiedi un'azione ("Invia un'email a Giovanni")
2. LIA prepara una bozza
3. Vedi una scheda con tutti i campi (destinatario, oggetto, corpo…)
4. Tre opzioni:
• ✅ Approva: l'azione viene eseguita
• ✏️ Modifica: correggi la bozza
• ❌ Annulla: non succede nulla

📋 Azioni interessate:
• Invio, risposta e inoltro di email
• Creazione, modifica ed eliminazione di eventi
• Creazione e modifica di contatti
• Creazione e completamento di attività
• Eliminazione di email

🛡️ Vantaggi:
• Verifica prima di ogni azione importante
• Possibilità di correggere gli errori
• Controllo totale sui tuoi dati
• Nessuna azione irreversibile senza il tuo consenso

📚 Più bozze alla volta:
Chiedi due email nella stessa frase: LIA elenca prima ciò che ha preparato, poi mostra una bozza alla volta ("Bozza 1 di 2"), ciascuna con la sua scheda e i propri Approva / Modifica / Annulla. Non parte nulla prima della tua ultima risposta, e il resoconto dice cosa è partito e a chi — anche una bozza annullata vi compare. 2. 你看到一张卡片，列出所有字段（收件人、主题、正文……）
3. 你可以：批准、编辑或取消
4. 只有在你明确批准后才会执行操作

在一句话里要求两封邮件：LIA 先列出它准备好的内容，然后一次显示一份草稿（"第 1 份草稿，共 2 份"），每份都有自己的卡片和自己的批准 / 编辑 / 取消。在你最后一次回答之前什么都不会发出，报告会说明发给了谁、发了什么——被取消的草稿也会列出。你已经以列表形式批准的批量操作（"删除这 5 封邮件"）仍只需一次确认。

✉️ 一个例外：
发给你自己的邮件无需草稿即可发出：收件人是你自己的地址，任何东西都改变不了它——即使是混进 LIA 所读邮件里的一段文字也不行。

old:
提示作为代码管理

LIA使用版本化提示系统，每个提示是存储在src/domains/agents/prompts/v1/中的文本文件。这种方法提供版本控制、代码审查和可追溯性。

155个按类别的专业提示

系统包含155个按类别分布的提示文件：

  • 流水线核心 — query_analyzer（路由）、smart_planner、response、semantic_validator、semantic_pivot、compaction
  • 领域智能体（17） — brave、browser、calendar、contacts、drive、emails、health、hue、perplexity、places、query、routes、tasks、weather、web_fetch、web_search、wikipedia
  • ReAct 循环 — react_agent、subagent_react、skill_react、mcp_react
  • HITL — classifier（含按操作类型的示例）、draft_critique、plan_approval、question_generator、draft_modifier
  • 记忆与心理 — 提取、引用解析、行为指令、心理自评与体现
  • 主动性 — heartbeat decision/message、initiative、兴趣、提醒
  • 日志与简报 — 内省、整合、每日问候与综述
  • 身份与翻译 — app_identity、default_personality、广播/技能/个性翻译

智能加载与动态检测

提示通过load_prompt()加载——不存在回退加载器：一个提示只有一个文本，即它的版本化文件。系统通过扫描文件系统中匹配v[0-9]+模式的目录来动态检测可用版本。带SHA256哈希验证的LRU缓存检测修改。版本可通过环境变量配置（如：RESPONSE_PROMPT_VERSION=v1），而且每个这类设置都有读取方，由测试核验。

提示加载器实践

系统使用LRU缓存和SHA256哈希验证：

@lru_cache(maxsize=256)
def load_prompt(
    name: PromptName,
    version: PromptVersion = "v1",
    validate_hash: bool = False,
    expected_hash: str | None = None,
) -> str:
    prompt_file = PROMPTS_DIR / version / f"{name}.txt"
    content = prompt_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

    if validate_hash and expected_hash:
        actual_hash = hashlib.sha256(
            content.encode("utf-8")
        ).hexdigest()
        if actual_hash != expected_hash:
            raise PromptIntegrityError(...)

    return content

与供应商无关的提示词缓存

每个动态系统提示词都用规范标记 --- DYNAMIC CONTEXT --- 将静态前缀（角色、规则、示例、输出格式）与按请求变化的内容分开。模板保持模型中立：基础设施层把这一约定翻译成各供应商的缓存方言——Anthropic 的 cache_control 块、OpenAI 的 prompt_cache_key 路由、其他供应商的隐式前缀缓存——从而在重复请求中减少计费 token 并降低延迟。作为流水线中最昂贵的提示词，planner 暴露约 77% 逐字节稳定的可缓存前缀，只减不增的 CI 守卫（标记必需、标记前不得有占位符、字节稳定性受断言保护）确保这一约定不会倒退。

提示词只陈述代码所强制的内容

模型读到的必须是真实的，而提示词是一句断言最容易偏离应用它的代码的地方。因此，提示词文件中的每个 {placeholder} 都在加载它的模块里有生产者，并由守卫同时读取两者；包含 {{ 的文件由 .format() 渲染，绝不用会把它原样留下的替换方式。每个上下文只有一条指令，写在文件里，且只在内容存在时才输出——空轮次不带任何空包裹，也不带关于并不存在的文档的规则。提示词公布的上限就是工具强制的上限，来自同一个常量；数字来自设置，事实来自应用它的代码，能力只有在本轮能够运行时才会被承诺。散文从不存放在 Python 里，备用文本也不：单行脚手架存放在由唯一解析器读取的 键|模板 行文件中，而文件缺失意味着部署损坏，应当大声失败，而不是悄悄换一种措辞。

提示注入：安全原则

注入提示中的外部内容（邮件、网页）封装在安全标签中，以防止提示注入攻击。提示也被设计为能够抵御操纵尝试。

old:
能，而且不靠心算。

🧮 计算：
• "1,234.56 欧元的 17.5% 是多少？"
• "把 1,550 欧元平分给四个人"
LIA 以精确的十进制计算：0.1 + 0.2 等于 0.3。结果不得不四舍五入时——除不尽的除法、开方——它会说明（「约」）。

📅 日期：
• "离 7 月 14 日还有几天？"
• "从今天起加 10 个工作日"
• "东京现在几点？"
工作日为周一至周五，不扣除法定节假日——它会说明。以小时计的时长按实际经过的时间计算，包括夏令时切换。

💱 货币：
• "250 美元是多少欧元？"
采用欧洲中央银行的参考汇率，LIA 会给出该汇率的日期。银行或信用卡会使用自己的汇率并收取费用：这是一个可靠的数量级，而不是你账单上的金额。

这些计算在 Pipeline 模式和 ReAct 模式下都能使用，无需任何设置。

msg: feat: add commit-anchored workspace memory
old:
UniGrok is a unified Grok agent: one gateway to xAI's Grok models with server-side web/X search and sandboxed code execution, plus local file, git, and test tools, and persistent session memory.

Start with the `agent` tool — it is the headline entry point. Give it any nontrivial task and it auto-routes across Grok models, runs tools as needed, and returns structured execution metadata. Use `chat` for plain conversation when you want to pin a model, `chat_with_vision` for images, `chat_with_files` to ground answers on uploaded documents, and `grok_reflect` when you need a focused structured critique without a tool loop.

Media: `generate_image`, `generate_video`, `extend_video` create with Grok Imagine. Cloud files: the `xai_*` tools manage uploads on xAI's servers, while `read_local_file`/`list_project_files` inspect the local workspace. Git: `git_status`/`git_diff`/`git_log`/`git_show` are read-only; write tools are gated behind local runtime flags. `web_search`/`x_search` answer real-time questions with citations, and `remote_code_execution` solves tasks in xAI's Python sandbox. Long-running research: `submit_research_job` starts a deferred background job (poll `get_research_job`), while `agent` mode='research' fans out multi-agent research inline with cited sources. Knowledge memory: `remember_fact`/`search_knowledge`/`forget_fact` manage durable distilled facts that auto-inject into matching prompts, and `distill_session` condenses a chat session into facts in the background.

msg: Templates create managed agents through agent management (CHOO-3481) (#851)
old:
# Switch templates, for agents

A template is one YAML document. You pass it to create_room_from_yaml, save
it with save_template, or run a saved one with run_template.

## Top-level keys

- version: the format version, 1.
- params: the inputs, each written as {name} anywhere else in the document.
- room: one room to create.
- group + rooms (+ links): a room group, its rooms, and links between them.
- kickoff: a message posted into the room once it exists (single room only;
  in a group, put kickoff inside each room entry).
- agent / agents: agents to create. Only Switch Console creates agents. To
  run such a template yourself, fill every agent it describes with an agent
  that already exists: run_template(agents={slot name: agent name}).

## A room

room:
  name: text
  description: text              # required
  instructions: text             # standing brief for the room's agents
  bridge: messaging app display name, or "{param}"
  channel_type: channel_public | channel_private
  agents: [agent names that exist on the server]
  users: [usernames on the room's messaging app; "{$creator}" is the deployer]
  aliases: {agent name: alias}   # @alias addresses that agent in this room

Without bridge the room goes on the server's default messaging app. users
needs the room to be on a messaging app.

## A group

group: {name: text, description: text}
rooms:
  - {name: ..., description: ..., agents: [...], kickoff: "@agent start"}
links:
  - {from: room name, to: room name, label: text}

## Params

params:
  <name>:
    type: string | number | boolean | enum | agent | bridge | room | user
    description: text
    default: a value, or for agent/bridge/room a list of candidates tried in
             order, where $first means the first one the server has
    required: true | false       # default: false with a single default value,
                                 # true with none or with a list of candidates
    enum: [choices]              # enum only
    pattern: regex               # string only, whole value must match
    min: number, max: number     # number only

provider, location and directory params are the Console's. run_template
drops them from an agent or team template; in a document you write yourself,
leave them out, since the server reads them as text and requires a value
like any other param. Give values in the inputs argument; a required param
with no value is refused with its name.

## Placeholders

{param} is replaced by the param's value; a field that is exactly one
placeholder keeps the value's type. Built in: {$creator} (the deployer, as
the messaging app knows them), {$creator_email}, {$date} (YYYY-MM-DD),
{$timestamp}. A {word} that names nothing is left as written.

## Kickoff

An agent starts working when a message addresses it, so mention each agent
the room needs: kickoff: "@helper start on the brief."
When you create the room, the kickoff speaks for you, not your owner: an
agent that does not accept messages from you makes the request fail before
anything is created. The kickoff also carries the run so far. Asking again
for a room with the same kickoff you already used further up the same path
pauses the run until your owner lets it continue.

## Example

version: 1
params:
  topic: {type: string, description: What the room is about}
room:
  name: "{topic} review"
  description: "Reviewing {topic}"
  agents: [reviewer]
  users: ["{$creator}"]
kickoff: "@reviewer read the brief and list three risks in {topic}."
new:
# Switch templates, for agents

A template is one YAML document that says what to create: agents, rooms, a
group of rooms. You run one you write with create_room_from_yaml, save it
with save_template, or run a saved one with run_template. Write new
templates in version 2, described here; "Version 1" at the end is for
reading older ones.

## The shape

version: 2
params:      # the inputs, each written as {name} anywhere below
  <name>: {type: ..., default: ..., ...}
resources:   # what the template creates, each under a key with a type
  <key>:     # letters, digits and _
    type: agent | room | group
    if: "{param}" | "{param} == value" | "{param} != value"   # optional
    ...the fields of that type
form:        # optional: how the form folds things away
  advanced: {label: Advanced, open: false}

Resources refer to each other by key: a room's agents: [lead] lists the
agent whose key is lead, and {lead.name} anywhere is the name that resource
is created under (an agent's name, or the identifier its display_name
gives). A reference to a resource whose if: does not hold is refused.

## if:, the one conditional

- On a resource: it is created only while the condition holds.
- On a param: it is asked only while the condition holds. A param that is
  not asked reads as empty, and drops out of the lists it was written in.
- In a field's value, as a list: the first entry whose if holds is taken,
  and an entry with no if always holds:
    addressing:
      - {if: "{start_in} == new_room", value: {anyone_in: [lead_room]}}
      - {value: anyone}

A condition reads one param: "{param}" (true when it has a value) or
"{param} == value" / "{param} != value".

## An agent (type: agent)

  instructions: text             # REQUIRED. The agent's brief.
  provider: claude | codex | opencode | "{param}"   # REQUIRED
  machine: machine name or id | "{param}"           # REQUIRED: where it runs
  directory: path | "{param}"                       # REQUIRED
  name: identifier               # optional; else derived from display_name.
                                 # Lowercase letters, digits, . - _
  display_name: text             # optional; how people see it
  description: text              # optional; what it is for
  model: text | "{param}"        # optional; the provider's default if absent
  advanced_config: {key: value}  # optional; see get_advanced_config(provider)
  isolation: shared | isolated   # optional; default shared
  auto_approve: true | false     # optional; default false
  addressing: owner | owner-agents | anyone | {anyone_in: [room keys]}
                                 # optional; default owner (only the deployer)
  connections:                   # optional; the deployer's connections it gets
    - {service: github, access: read | write, repos: [owner/name]}
    - atlassian                  #   or just the service's name
  repo: URL                      # optional; it clones it into its directory
                                 # (a private one needs a github connection)
  join: [existing room name or "{param}"]   # optional; rooms it is added to
  sources: [{label, url} or url] # optional; pages it should read
  allow_existing: true | false   # optional; an existing agent may stand in

Each agent is created as a managed agent of the deployer (your owner, when
you run it) on the machine it names, before the rooms. That needs agent
management on the server and, for you, the "can manage agents" capability;
the machine must be online with the provider installed and signed in. The
whole run is checked before anything is created; every problem comes back
with its reason code, and agents made before a later failure are deleted.

provider, machine and directory are never filled in for you: say each on the
agent, as a value or "{param}". A param offers a choice with a default:
machine default [$first] is the first online machine that can run the agents'
providers; provider default [claude, codex] the first ready on its machine;
directory "{$agents_dir}/{lead.name}" the agent's own folder on its machine.

connections are the deployer's own, granted to the new agent: they must have
connected each, with write access to grant write. anyone_in admits anyone in
those rooms of the run as well as the deployer. join adds the agent to rooms
that already exist; each must be one the deployer may add agents to.
allow_existing: true lets run_template(agents={key: existing agent name}) put
an agent that exists in the slot instead; leave it out unless asked.

Before saving an agent template, settle with the person who asked: which
coding agent runs each agent, on which machine, in which directory, what it
may reach (connections), who may talk to it (addressing), and whether an
existing agent may stand in for it.

## A room (type: room)

  name: text                     # REQUIRED
  description: text              # REQUIRED
  instructions: text             # standing brief for the room's agents
  bridge: messaging app display name, or "{param}"
  channel_type: channel_public | channel_private
  agents: [agent keys, or names of agents that exist]
  users: [usernames on its messaging app; "{$creator}" is the deployer]
  aliases: {agent key or name: alias}   # @alias addresses it in this room
  kickoff: text                  # posted once the room exists
  group: <group key>             # when the template has a group

Without bridge the room goes on the server's default messaging app; users
needs one (make them depend on it: [{if: "{bridge}", value: [...]},
{value: []}]). Several rooms go in one group.

## A group (type: group)

  name: text
  description: text
  links: [{from: room key, to: room key, label: text}]

## Params

  <name>:
    type: string | number | boolean | enum | agent | bridge | room | user
          | provider | machine | directory
    description: text
    label: text                  # the input's name on the form
    default: a value, or for agent/bridge/room/provider/machine a list of
             candidates tried in order, $first meaning the first that works
    required: true | false       # default: false with a single default value,
                                 # true with none or with a list of candidates
    input: ask | advanced | fixed  # shown, folded away, or not editable
    enum: [choices]              # enum only
    pattern: regex               # string only, whole value must match
    min: number, max: number     # number only
    multiline: true | false      # string only, a text area
    if: condition                # asked only while it holds

Give values in run_template's inputs argument; a required param with no value
is refused with its name.

## Placeholders

{param} is replaced by the param's value; a field that is exactly one
placeholder keeps the value's type. {key.name} is a resource's name. Built
in: {$creator} (the deployer, as the messaging app knows them),
{$creator_email}, {$date} (YYYY-MM-DD), {$timestamp}, and {$agents_dir} (the
folder an agent's machine keeps agents in). A {word} that names nothing is
left as written.

## Kickoff

An agent starts working when a message addresses it, so a room's kickoff
mentions each agent it needs: kickoff: "@{lead.name} start on the brief."
When you run the template, the kickoff speaks for you, not your owner: an
agent that would not accept messages from you makes the run fail before
anything is created (give a new agent addressing owner-agents, or anyone_in
its room). Asking again for a room with the same kickoff you already used
further up the same path pauses the run until your owner lets it continue.

## Example

version: 2
params:
  topic: {type: string, description: What the room is about}
resources:
  review:
    type: room
    name: "{topic} review"
    description: "Reviewing {topic}"
    agents: [reviewer]
    users: ["{$creator}"]
    kickoff: "@reviewer read the brief and list three risks in {topic}."

## Version 1

Older templates have no resources: and say what a block is by where it sits.
A top-level agent: or agents: list holds agents (each with location: local |
ssh host instead of machine: on a Console that runs them itself), room: one
room with a top-level kickoff:, and group: with rooms: and links: a group. A
room lists agents by the text written as their name, and in a single agent:
document {agent} is its name. They still run as they are; write new ones in
version 2.

old:
# Switch templates, for agents

A template is one YAML document that says what to create: agents, rooms, a
group of rooms. You run one you write with create_room_from_yaml, save it
with save_template, or run a saved one with run_template. Write new
templates in version 2, described here; "Version 1" at the end is for
reading older ones.

## The shape

version: 2
params:      # the inputs, each written as {name} anywhere below
  <name>: {type: ..., default: ..., ...}
resources:   # what the template creates, each under a key with a type
  <key>:     # letters, digits and _
    type: agent | room | group
    if: "{param}" | "{param} == value" | "{param} != value"   # optional
    ...the fields of that type
form:        # optional: how the form folds things away
  advanced: {label: Advanced, open: false}

Resources refer to each other by key: a room's agents: [lead] lists the
agent whose key is lead, and {lead.name} anywhere is the name that resource
is created under (an agent's name, or the identifier its display_name
gives). A reference to a resource whose if: does not hold is refused.

## if:, the one conditional

- On a resource: it is created only while the condition holds.
- On a param: it is asked only while the condition holds. A param that is
  not asked reads as empty, and drops out of the lists it was written in.
- In a field's value, as a list: the first entry whose if holds is taken,
  and an entry with no if always holds:
    addressing:
      - {if: "{start_in} == new_room", value: {anyone_in: [lead_room]}}
      - {value: anyone}

A condition reads one param: "{param}" (true when it has a value) or
"{param} == value" / "{param} != value".

## An agent (type: agent)

  instructions: text             # REQUIRED. The agent's brief.
  provider: claude | codex | opencode | "{param}"   # REQUIRED
  machine: machine name or id | "{param}"           # REQUIRED: where it runs
  directory: path | "{param}"                       # REQUIRED
  name: identifier               # optional; else derived from display_name.
                                 # Lowercase letters, digits, . - _
  display_name: text             # optional; how people see it
  description: text              # optional; what it is for
  model: text | "{param}"        # optional; the provider's default if absent
  advanced_config: {key: value}  # optional; see get_advanced_config(provider)
  isolation: shared | isolated   # optional; default shared
  auto_approve: true | false     # optional; default false
  addressing: owner | owner-agents | anyone | {anyone_in: [room keys]}
                                 # optional; default owner (only the deployer)
  connections:                   # optional; the deployer's connections it gets
    - {service: github, access: read | write, repos: [owner/name]}
    - atlassian                  #   or just the service's name
  repo: URL                      # optional; it clones it into its directory
                                 # (a private one needs a github connection)
  join: [existing room name or "{param}"]   # optional; rooms it is added to
  sources: [{label, url} or url] # optional; pages it should read
  allow_existing: true | false   # optional; an existing agent may stand in

Each agent is created as a managed agent of the deployer (your owner, when
you run it) on the machine it names, before the rooms. That needs agent
management on the server and, for you, the "can manage agents" capability;
the machine must be online with the provider installed and signed in. The
whole run is checked before anything is created; every problem comes back
with its reason code, and agents made before a later failure are deleted.

provider, machine and directory are never filled in for you: say each on the
agent, as a value or "{param}". A param offers a choice with a default:
machine default [$first] is the first online machine that can run the agents'
providers; provider default [claude, codex] the first ready on its machine;
directory "{$agents_dir}/{lead.name}" the agent's own folder on its machine.

connections are the deployer's own, granted to the new agent: they must have
connected each, with write access to grant write. anyone_in admits anyone in
those rooms of the run as well as the deployer. join adds the agent to rooms
that already exist; each must be one the deployer may add agents to.
allow_existing: true lets run_template(agents={key: existing agent name}) put
an agent that exists in the slot instead; leave it out unless asked.

Before saving an agent template, settle with the person who asked: which
coding agent runs each agent, on which machine, in which directory, what it
may reach (connections), who may talk to it (addressing), and whether an
existing agent may stand in for it.

## A room (type: room)

  name: text                     # REQUIRED
  description: text              # REQUIRED
  instructions: text             # standing brief for the room's agents
  bridge: messaging app display name, or "{param}"
  channel_type: channel_public | channel_private
  agents: [agent keys, or names of agents that exist]
  users: [usernames on its messaging app; "{$creator}" is the deployer]
  aliases: {agent key or name: alias}   # @alias addresses it in this room
  kickoff: text                  # posted once the room exists
  group: <group key>             # when the template has a group

Without bridge the room goes on the server's default messaging app; users
needs one (make them depend on it: [{if: "{bridge}", value: [...]},
{value: []}]). Several rooms go in one group.

## A group (type: group)

  name: text
  description: text
  links: [{from: room key, to: room key, label: text}]

## Params

  <name>:
    type: string | number | boolean | enum | agent | bridge | room | user
          | provider | machine | directory
    description: text
    label: text                  # the input's name on the form
    default: a value, or for agent/bridge/room/provider/machine a list of
             candidates tried in order, $first meaning the first that works
    required: true | false       # default: false with a single default value,
                                 # true with none or with a list of candidates
    input: ask | advanced | fixed  # shown, folded away, or not editable
    enum: [choices]              # enum only
    pattern: regex               # string only, whole value must match
    min: number, max: number     # number only
    multiline: true | false      # string only, a text area
    if: condition                # asked only while it holds

Give values in run_template's inputs argument; a required param with no value
is refused with its name.

## Placeholders

{param} is replaced by the param's value; a field that is exactly one
placeholder keeps the value's type. {key.name} is a resource's name. Built
in: {$creator} (the deployer, as the messaging app knows them),
{$creator_email}, {$date} (YYYY-MM-DD), {$timestamp}, and {$agents_dir} (the
folder an agent's machine keeps agents in). A {word} that names nothing is
left as written.

## Kickoff

An agent starts working when a message addresses it, so a room's kickoff
mentions each agent it needs: kickoff: "@{lead.name} start on the brief."
When you run the template, the kickoff speaks for you, not your owner: an
agent that would not accept messages from you makes the run fail before
anything is created (give a new agent addressing owner-agents, or anyone_in
its room). Asking again for a room with the same kickoff you already used
further up the same path pauses the run until your owner lets it continue.

## Example

version: 2
params:
  topic: {type: string, description: What the room is about}
resources:
  review:
    type: room
    name: "{topic} review"
    description: "Reviewing {topic}"
    agents: [reviewer]
    users: ["{$creator}"]
    kickoff: "@reviewer read the brief and list three risks in {topic}."

## Version 1

Older templates have no resources: and say what a block is by where it sits.
A top-level agent: or agents: list holds agents (each with location: local |
ssh host instead of machine: on a Console that runs them itself), room: one
room with a top-level kickoff:, and group: with rooms: and links: a group. A
room lists agents by the text written as their name, and in a single agent:
document {agent} is its name. They still run as they are; write new ones in
version 2.

You are a senior performance marketing strategist. Analyze the following
product brief using established copywriting frameworks to build a
comprehensive creative foundation for ad generation.

Product brief: {input.product_brief}
Brand voice (if provided): {input.brand_voice}

Perform each of the following analyses and output them as labeled sections:

1. AIDA FRAMEWORK MAPPING: Map the product to the Attention-Interest-
   Desire-Action framework. What grabs attention? What sustains interest?
   What creates desire? What drives the click/conversion action?

2. PAS FRAMEWORK MAPPING: Identify the core Problem the audience faces,
   Agitate it by describing the emotional and practical consequences of
   inaction, then position the product as the Solution.

3. UNIQUE SELLING PROPOSITIONS: List 3-5 USPs ranked by differentiation
   strength. For each USP, note whether it is feature-based, benefit-based,
   or emotion-based, and rate its defensibility (easy/hard to copy).

4. AUDIENCE SEGMENTS: Define 2-3 distinct audience micro-segments with
   their demographics, psychographics, primary pain points, objection
   patterns, and preferred messaging tone.

5. EMOTIONAL TRIGGERS: Identify the top 5 emotional triggers (e.g. fear
   of missing out, aspiration, trust, curiosity, belonging) and map each
   to a specific product benefit or proof point.

6. COMPETITIVE POSITIONING: Summarize what makes this product different
   from likely alternatives. Note any claims that need substantiation
   (statistics, certifications, awards).

and statistical testing methodology. Create a detailed A/B testing
plan for the generated ad variants.

Build a structured A/B TESTING PLAN with these sections:

1. TEST PRIORITY MATRIX: Rank all 10 variants (5 Google + 5 Meta)
   by predicted impact and ease of testing. Use a 2x2 matrix:
   High Impact/Easy to Test (do first) through Low Impact/Hard to Test.

   - Phase 1 (Week 1-2): Which 2 ad groups to test head-to-head?
   - Phase 2 (Week 3-4): Winner vs. next challenger
   - Minimum sample size per variant (assume 2% baseline CTR)
   - Statistical significance threshold (recommend 95% confidence)
   - Primary KPI: CTR. Secondary KPIs: conversion rate, CPA, ROAS

3. META ADS TEST SEQUENCE:
   - Phase 1 (Week 1-2): Which 2 creative approaches to test?
   - Phase 2 (Week 3-4): Winning copy x 3 different visual creatives
   - Recommended daily budget per variant ($X minimum for significance)
   - Campaign Budget Optimization (CBO) vs. Ad Set Budget recommendations
   - Primary KPI: Thumb-stop rate + CTR. Secondary: CPM, CPA

4. BUDGET ALLOCATION: Recommend initial budget split across platforms
   and variants. Include a reallocation trigger (e.g. "shift 70% budget
   to winner after 1000 impressions per variant with >95% confidence").

5. PERFORMANCE PREDICTION: For each variant, predict expected CTR
   range (low/mid/high) with reasoning. Flag any variants that may
   face policy review issues on either platform.

6. ITERATION ROADMAP: Based on likely test outcomes, suggest the next
   3 rounds of creative iterations (e.g. headline swaps, CTA tests,
   audience expansion tests).

new:
Parse all API endpoints from the source files into a structured catalog.

Source files: {steps.fetch-specs.output}

For each endpoint discovered, extract the following with maximum precision:

1. **Method** - GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS
2. **Path** - URL path with parameter placeholders using OpenAPI syntax (e.g. /users/{id})
   Include any path prefix from router mounting or API versioning (e.g. /api/v2/users/{id})
3. **Summary** - one-line description of what the endpoint does
4. **Description** - detailed explanation from comments, docstrings, or decorators.
   If no description exists, infer from function name, parameter names, and return types.
5. **Parameters:**
   - Path parameters: name, type (string/integer/uuid), required=true, description, format
   - Query parameters: name, type, required flag, default value, description, enum values
   - Header parameters: custom headers, Accept/Content-Type variants, API version headers
6. **Request body** - full schema with field names, types, required flags, constraints
   (min/max, pattern, enum), nested object schemas, and realistic example values.
   Note content type: application/json, multipart/form-data, application/x-www-form-urlencoded
7. **Response schemas** - for EVERY status code the endpoint can return:
   - 2xx success responses (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content) with body schema
   - 400 Bad Request: validation error format (field-level errors, error codes)
   - 401 Unauthorized: missing/invalid authentication response format
   - 403 Forbidden: insufficient permissions response
   - 404 Not Found: resource not found response format
   - 409 Conflict: duplicate resource or state conflict
   - 422 Unprocessable Entity: business logic validation errors
   - 429 Too Many Requests: rate limit exceeded response with Retry-After header
   - 500 Internal Server Error: generic error envelope format
   For each, provide the response body schema AND a realistic example.
8. **Authentication requirements:**
   - Method: Bearer JWT, API key (header/query), OAuth 2.0 (which flows), session cookie
   - Required scopes or permissions (e.g. "users:read", "admin")
   - Whether endpoint is publicly accessible or requires auth
9. **Rate limiting:**
   - Requests per window (e.g. 100/minute, 1000/hour)
   - Rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset)
   - Whether limits are per-key, per-IP, or per-user
10. **Tags/Groups** - logical grouping (users, billing, admin, etc.)
11. **Deprecation** - flag any deprecated endpoints with sunset date if available

Organize endpoints by group/tag. Within each group, order by path then method.
Flag any endpoints with incomplete documentation (missing descriptions, no response schema).
Track documentation completeness percentage per endpoint.

Return a comprehensive JSON catalog of all endpoints.

10=catastrophic). The composite risk score = likelihood x impact (1-100).

CLAUSE-BY-CLAUSE RISK ASSESSMENT:

1. LIABILITY AND INDEMNIFICATION RISKS:
   - Are liability caps reasonable for the contract value? Industry standard is
     typically 1-2x annual contract value for direct damages.
   - Is there an uncapped indemnification obligation? Flag any indemnity without
     aggregate caps as HIGH risk.
   - Are consequential damages excluded mutually or one-sided?
   - Does the indemnification procedure require timely notice and cooperation?
   - Check for "hold harmless" language that may exceed standard indemnification.

2. TERMINATION AND LOCK-IN RISKS:
   - Auto-renewal without adequate opt-out notice (< 60 days is risky).
   - Termination for convenience penalties that exceed reasonable breakage costs.
   - Missing or inadequate transition assistance provisions.
   - Data portability and return obligations upon termination.
   - "Evergreen" clauses that make exit prohibitively expensive.

3. FINANCIAL RISKS:
   - Unlimited price escalation mechanisms or uncapped CPI adjustments.
   - Payment terms that create cash flow exposure (net-90+ is elevated risk).
   - Missing audit rights on usage-based or variable pricing.
   - Penalty clauses that may be unenforceable or disproportionate.

4. IP AND CONFIDENTIALITY RISKS:
   - Overly broad IP assignment that captures pre-existing IP.
   - Work-for-hire provisions on materials that should remain licensed.
   - Confidentiality obligations without reasonable carve-outs (public info, compelled disclosure).
   - Non-compete scope that unreasonably restricts future business.

5. OPERATIONAL RISKS:
   - SLAs without meaningful remedies (credits, termination rights).
   - Force majeure that is too narrow or too broad.
   - Assignment restrictions that block M&A transactions.
   - Missing or one-sided audit rights.

6. MARKET STANDARD COMPARISON:
   - Compare each material clause against industry-standard benchmarks.
   - Flag terms that deviate significantly from what a reasonably sophisticated
     party would accept in an arm's-length negotiation.
   - Note any "unusual" provisions not commonly seen in this contract type.

Validate the extracted data using a multi-layer validation framework.

LAYER 1 - COMPLETENESS CHECK:
- Compare extracted fields against the expected field list from document analysis.
- Flag any "required" fields that are missing (required fields depend on document type:
  invoices MUST have: vendor, invoice_number, date, total; receipts MUST have: merchant,
  date, total; contracts MUST have: parties, effective_date, governing_law).
- Calculate completeness percentage: (fields_extracted / fields_expected) x 100.

LAYER 2 - FORMAT VALIDATION:
- Dates: verify valid calendar dates (no Feb 30, no month 13), check logical order
  (start_date before end_date, invoice_date before due_date).
- Numbers: verify non-negative where expected, check reasonable ranges (e.g., tax rate
  0-100%, quantity > 0, unit_price > 0).
- Emails: validate format (contains @, valid domain structure).
- Phone numbers: validate against expected format for the detected country.
- Postal codes: validate format against detected country.
- Currency: verify consistency (all amounts in same currency unless multi-currency noted).

LAYER 3 - CROSS-FIELD CONSISTENCY:
- Arithmetic checks: line_item_quantities x unit_prices = line_totals,
  sum(line_totals) = subtotal, subtotal + tax = total.
- Tolerance: allow 0.01 rounding difference for financial calculations.
- Logical consistency: shipping_date >= order_date, end_date >= start_date.
- Reference consistency: IDs mentioned in different sections match.
- Party consistency: names and addresses are consistent across document sections.

LAYER 4 - ANOMALY DETECTION:
- Statistical outliers: values that are >3 standard deviations from expected ranges
  for this document type (e.g., invoice total $1M when typical is $1K-$10K).
- Duplicate detection: identical line items, repeated reference numbers.
- Suspicious patterns: sequential invoice numbers with large gaps, dates far in the
  future or past, amounts that are exact round numbers when decimals expected.

the email is opened or ignored - it is the most important element of
the entire campaign. Generate high-performing subject line variants.

Audience brief: {steps.audience-brief.output}
Campaign type: {input.campaign_type}

Generate 8 SUBJECT LINE VARIANTS using different proven techniques:

1. CURIOSITY GAP: Creates an information gap the reader must open to
   resolve. Example: "The one metric most marketers ignore"
   - Subject: [max 50 chars] - show count [XX/50]
   - Preview text: [max 90 chars] - show count [XX/90]
   (Preview text = first line of email body OR explicit preheader)

2. URGENCY/SCARCITY: Time-limited or quantity-limited framing.
   Example: "Last chance: 40% off ends tonight"
   - Subject + preview text with counts

3. PERSONALIZATION: Uses recipient's name, company, or behavior data.
   Example: "[First Name], your Q2 benchmark report is ready"
   - Subject + preview text with counts

4. BENEFIT-DRIVEN: Leads with the value the reader will get.
   Example: "Cut your onboarding time by 60%"
   - Subject + preview text with counts

5. SOCIAL PROOF: References others' behavior or endorsements.
   Example: "Why 10,000+ teams switched this quarter"
   - Subject + preview text with counts

6. QUESTION: Asks something the reader wants answered.
   Example: "Are you making this common pricing mistake?"
   - Subject + preview text with counts

7. NUMBER/LIST: Uses a specific number for concreteness.
   Example: "7 templates that doubled our response rate"
   - Subject + preview text with counts

8. CONTRARIAN/PROVOCATIVE: Challenges conventional wisdom.
   Example: "Stop doing X (here's what works instead)"
   - Subject + preview text with counts

FOR EACH VARIANT ALSO PROVIDE:

You are an email copywriter specializing in narrative-driven emotional
copy. Write email Variant B using a storytelling approach that builds
connection before conversion.

Audience brief: {steps.audience-brief.output}
Campaign type: {input.campaign_type}

WRITE THE EMAIL FOLLOWING THIS STRUCTURE:

1. PREHEADER TEXT (40-90 characters): Complement the subject line with
   a curiosity hook or emotional teaser.

2. OPENING STORY (3-5 sentences): Start with a relatable scenario or
   customer story that mirrors the reader's experience. Use specific
   details (names, numbers, situations) to make it feel real.
   Frameworks to choose from:
   - "Before/After": Paint the painful before, hint at the beautiful after
   - "The Moment": "Last Tuesday, Sarah realized she'd spent 6 hours on
     something that should take 20 minutes..."
   - "The Question": Start with a question that makes the reader nod
   The goal: make the reader think "that's exactly my situation."

3. THE BRIDGE (2-3 sentences): Transition from the story's problem to
   your solution. This is the "but then everything changed" moment.
   Keep it natural - not salesy. The product should feel like a
   discovery, not a pitch.

   - A short customer testimonial (2-3 sentences with name and title)

   step in the story, not a hard sell.

   Place the CTA where it naturally follows the story's resolution.

6. P.S. LINE: Add a P.S. at the bottom (research shows 79% of readers
   scan directly to the P.S.). Use it for:
   - A deadline reminder ("P.S. This offer expires Friday at midnight")
   - A secondary benefit not mentioned above
   - A personal touch from the sender

7. FOOTER: Same compliance requirements as Variant A.

  words). No sentences over 25 words.
- Use "you" at least 3x more than "we" or "our"

   - Angle: Limited time offer or expiring access

new:
You are a DEI (Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion) specialist and
organizational psychologist. Perform a rigorous bias audit on the
following job description. Your goal is to maximize the diversity
of qualified applicants.

Job description: {steps.write-jd.output}

Audit the following dimensions and flag EVERY instance found:

1. GENDERED LANGUAGE: Scan for masculine-coded words (aggressive,
   dominant, competitive, rock star, ninja, crushing it) and
   feminine-coded words (supportive, nurturing, collaborative -
   which can signal the role is undervalued). Use the Gaucher et al.
   (2011) gendered wording research as a reference. List each word
   found with a neutral replacement.

2. AGE-CODED TERMS: Flag "digital native", "young and hungry",
   "recent graduate", "5+ years" when the role doesn't truly need it,
   "high energy", "startup mentality". Each one discourages older or
   younger candidates depending on direction.

3. ABLEIST LANGUAGE: Check for physical ability assumptions like
   "must be able to lift 50 lbs" (when not actually required),
   "walks clients through", "stand-up meetings" used literally.

4. UNNECESSARY BARRIERS:
   - Degree requirements: Is a bachelor's/master's truly required,
     or would equivalent experience suffice? (Google, Apple, IBM
     have all dropped degree requirements for most roles.)
   - Certification requirements: Are they legally required or just
     preferred?
   - Experience inflation: Is "7+ years" actually needed, or would
     "3-5 years" suffice for the actual responsibilities listed?
   - Tool-specific requirements: Is "must know Jira" a real need,
     or is "experience with project management tools" sufficient?

5. CULTURAL EXCLUSION: Check for phrases that assume specific cultural
   backgrounds ("beer Fridays", "ping-pong table", "work hard play
   hard", religious holiday assumptions in benefits).

6. READABILITY: Run a Flesch-Kincaid assessment. Job descriptions
   above grade 10 reading level lose 50%+ of applicants. Flag any
   sentences that are overly complex or use unnecessary jargon.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
- ISSUES FOUND: Numbered list with original text, issue type, and
  suggested replacement
- CORRECTED JOB DESCRIPTION: Full rewritten version with all fixes
- BIAS SCORE: Rate the original 1-10 (10 = fully inclusive) and the
  corrected version similarly
- CHANGE SUMMARY: Brief list of all modifications made

Keep a Changelog standard (https://keepachangelog.com/) combined with semantic
versioning awareness.

CATEGORIZATION (Keep a Changelog standard):
- **Added**: New features, new endpoints, new CLI commands, new configuration options
- **Changed**: Changes to existing functionality, API behavior changes, UI modifications
- **Deprecated**: Features marked for removal in a future version
- **Removed**: Features or capabilities that have been removed
- **Fixed**: Bug fixes, error corrections, crash fixes
- **Security**: Vulnerability patches, dependency security updates, auth fixes

ADDITIONAL INTERNAL CATEGORIES:
- **Performance**: Optimizations, caching improvements, query tuning
- **Infrastructure**: CI/CD changes, deployment configs, Docker updates, dependency bumps
- **Refactored**: Code restructuring with no behavior change (internal only)

FOR EACH CHANGE, EXTRACT:
- Short summary (1 line, imperative mood: "Add X" not "Added X" or "Adds X")
- Detailed description (2-3 sentences explaining the what and why)
- Affected components/modules (e.g., "API", "Dashboard", "CLI", "Database")
- PR or commit reference if identifiable from the diff
- Severity: major (breaking or high-impact), minor (new feature), patch (fix/improvement)

SEMANTIC VERSIONING ASSESSMENT:
Based on the changes, recommend the version bump:
- MAJOR (X.0.0): if any breaking changes are present
- MINOR (0.X.0): if new features added with no breaking changes
- PATCH (0.0.X): if only fixes and non-functional improvements
Explain the reasoning for the version recommendation.

BREAKING CHANGE DETECTION:
For each change, explicitly check:
- Does it change an API endpoint URL, method, or response schema?
- Does it rename or remove a configuration option or environment variable?
- Does it change default behavior that users may depend on?
- Does it require database migration or data transformation?
- Does it drop support for a previously supported platform, runtime, or browser?
Flag any breaking change with a "BREAKING:" prefix and severity assessment.

Changes: {input.changelog}

set for this specific candidate. Create interview questions that
efficiently validate the most important unknowns.

Design interview questions in these categories:

1. GAP VERIFICATION QUESTIONS (top priority - 3-4 questions):
   For each identified skill gap or partial match, design a question
   that assesses whether the candidate has more depth than the resume
   shows, or can learn quickly:
   - Question text (behavioral or situational format)
   - What to listen for (strong answer indicators)
   - Red flag answers (concerning responses)
   - Follow-up probe to go deeper

2. ACHIEVEMENT VERIFICATION QUESTIONS (3-4 questions):
   For the candidate's top claimed achievements, design questions
   using the STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to
   verify the scope of their contribution:
   - "Tell me about [specific achievement]. What was your specific
     role vs. the team's contribution?"
   - Probe for: metrics, timelines, obstacles, and what they'd do
     differently
   - Look for: specificity (real experience) vs. vagueness (inflated)

3. GROWTH POTENTIAL ASSESSMENT (2-3 questions):
   - "Describe a time you had to learn something completely new in a
     short timeframe. How did you approach it?"
   - "What's the biggest professional mistake you've made, and what
     did you change as a result?"
   - Design questions that assess learning agility, self-awareness,
     and adaptability

4. ROLE-SPECIFIC SCENARIO (1-2 questions):

     90 days of this role
   - The scenario should test their approach to a real problem, not
     their theoretical knowledge
   - Include a scoring guide (1-4 scale with behavioral anchors)

5. CANDIDATE'S QUESTIONS: Suggest 2-3 topics the interviewer should
   be prepared to answer about (based on what a candidate with this
   profile would likely care about - compensation, growth path, team
   dynamics, technical stack, etc.)

age, race, religion, marital/family status, disability, national
origin, genetic information, or pregnancy status.
